claims.text: Rapid quenching during nanoparticle synthesis kinetically restricts atomic diffusion.
Restricting diffusion by rapid quenching freezes a disordered high-entropy state.
The quenched disordered state preserves a homogeneous solid solution during high-temperature catalytic and thermoelectric service.
Slow cooling permits more atomic diffusion than rapid quenching.
The additional atomic mobility during slow cooling enables elemental ordering, phase separation, or incipient intermetallic formation.
Ordering, phase separation, or intermetallic formation diminishes the structural and chemical stability of the nanoparticles.
The relevant structural mediator is the degree of atomic randomness versus phase segregation or intermetallic bonding.
Rapidly quenched nanoparticles will retain a more homogeneous solid solution and show less phase segregation after thermal exposure than slow-cooled nanoparticles.
Slow-cooled nanoparticles will show elemental segregation or incipient intermetallic formation after high-temperature exposure.
The processing-dependent differences should become most pronounced at temperatures approaching or exceeding 773 K because atomic diffusion becomes activated.
Even when service temperatures activate diffusion, phase-separation kinetics remain influenced by the structural state established during synthesis.
Differences between rapidly quenched and slowly cooled nanoparticles should be less significant at lower service temperatures.
Nanoparticle size distribution can affect the observed processing-dependent stability.
Minor compositional variability can affect the observed processing-dependent stability.
